scope: Authored summaries at inspected loci. Direct textual presence, published findings and attributed reconstructions remain distinct.

observations.locus: Printed pp. 9–10; first excerpt PDF pp. 9–10
observations.statement: The introduction describes poet-patron exchange and attributes the poet’s social position and patronage role to Indo-Iranian and Indo-European inheritance.
observations.rival_bearing: R2 supplies an ancestral explanation for this role; local contributions to particular practices remain possible.
observations.inference_limit: The claim is a comparative argument, not an observed Bronze Age teacher chain or proof that every institutional feature is inherited.

observations.locus: Printed p. 5 and pp. 14–17; first PDF p. 5, second PDF pp. 2–5
observations.statement: The authors separate hymn composition from older conventions, family collections, later consolidation and school recensions; the Kuru consolidation is attributed to Witzel.
observations.rival_bearing: R2 and R5 can both contribute; a received canon can combine materials of different ages.
observations.inference_limit: The approximate composition estimate does not date every represented practice, and collection dates remain scholarly estimates.

observations.locus: Printed p. 14; second excerpt PDF p. 2
observations.statement: The introduction describes shared underlying poetic formulae and identifies parallels in Old Avestan while allowing creative changes to their verbal realization.
observations.rival_bearing: R2 concerns formula history; R5 can reorganize inherited verbal material.
observations.inference_limit: A formula comparison does not by itself trace the technical content of an agricultural image.

observations.locus: Yasna 45.1, lesson Text 3; printed/PDF p. 35, reinforced p. 101
observations.statement: The edited stanza addresses listeners approaching from near and far and presents a proclamation linked to cosmic order.
observations.kind: presence in an edited Old Avestan passage
observations.rival_bearing: Organized addressed speech exists in this Iranian comparator; broad teaching sophistication is not uniquely diagnostic of a local urban source.
observations.inference_limit: The represented audience is not an excavated school, a dated examination or a surveyed institution.

observations.statement: The lesson gives zaotā as a libator associated with ritual order and desirable action; its translation retains an uncertain divine referent.
observations.kind: edited role term and qualified translation
observations.rival_bearing: A ritual-specialist role supplies an Iranian control relevant to R2.
observations.inference_limit: The verse does not enumerate a historical human staffing pattern or authenticate a local institutional donor.

observations.statement: The passages connect divine fashioning, a cow’s choice, a cattle tender or forager, herds and thought in the edition’s interpretation.
observations.rival_bearing: A pastoral conceptual comparator is available; R2/R4 remain plausible for broad relations.
observations.inference_limit: These selected phrases specify no ploughing, seed-processing or water-lifting sequence and cannot serve as its operation match.

observations.statement: The translated passage places Vištāspa with song, gift exchange and audition; the surrounding translated verse retains uncertainty about the named generous figure.
observations.rival_bearing: A poet-support relationship is represented; a teaching or patronage setting need not be uniquely local.
observations.inference_limit: The presence of a name does not establish an independently dated royal patron or a literal teacher genealogy.

observations.statement: Boyce attributes a common origin to basic haoma/soma ritual similarities while recording later differences.
observations.rival_bearing: R2 is an available account for the shared ritual core.
observations.inference_limit: The reconstructed common core does not date all subsequently described ingredients, officiants or ritual operations.

observations.locus: Opening account identification and paragraph on the second parahōm preparation
observations.statement: The detailed account summarizes Bhagaria performance described by Kotwal; links to Old Avestan modifications are stated as suggestions and possibilities.
observations.rival_bearing: R5 and later elaboration affect the received ritual account.
observations.inference_limit: Modern observation, Young Avestan prescription and a proposed early change have different evidential status.
observations.source_anchor: It is this account which is summarized here

observations.statement: The northernmost South Asian transect begins around 1200 BCE; the IVC-related profile is modeled partly from individuals at culturally connected sites.
observations.rival_bearing: Demographic continuity or contact can supply opportunity for R1/R3.
observations.inference_limit: The source does not observe a feature-specific teacher, taught recipe or literary transfer.

observations.statement: The authors describe ancestry arrows as plausible directions and say sampling does not determine exact routes; the figure marks South Asian entry uncertain.
observations.rival_bearing: Possible contacts are compatible with several activity-specific routes.
observations.inference_limit: An ancestry arrow cannot be used as the observed route of a particular institution.

observations.locus: PDF p. 12, article p. 11, modern-group comparison
observations.statement: The priestly-group comparison is qualified by shared ancestry, nonblinded selection and potentially changing group classification.
observations.kind: published limitations on an attributed inference
observations.rival_bearing: The finding can inform population history while institutional descent requires additional premises.
observations.inference_limit: Present classifications cannot be silently assigned to sampled Bronze Age offices.

observations.locus: PDF p. 13, article p. 12, Dravidian discussion
observations.statement: The discussion presents both IVC-associated and southern/eastern explanations of proto-Dravidian spread using genetic, archaeological and linguistic premises.
observations.rival_bearing: Several historical routes remain in the source’s own argument.
observations.inference_limit: No scenario authenticates an Indus sign reading or identifies a transferred technical operation.

observations.statement: Witzel describes locally accepted school canons and links school differentiation to area, community, ritual and pronunciation.
observations.rival_bearing: R5 can consolidate distinct local verbal and ritual traditions.
observations.inference_limit: The source’s cited medieval manuscript estimate is not the date of composition or a modern census of every surviving witness.

observations.statement: The chapter distinguishes family-book collection from later rearrangement and argues that Kuru-era ritual and political consolidation brought traditions together.
observations.rival_bearing: R5 supplies a mechanism for mature combinations in a received corpus.
observations.inference_limit: The Kuru setting is a scholarly reconstruction; it does not imply every incorporated component originated then.

observations.statement: The summary discusses neighboring-school influence and later comprehensive compilations while stating that final compilation and redaction dates often remain unknown.
observations.kind: attributed synthesis with explicit chronological limits
observations.rival_bearing: R3/R5 may interact within the history of Vedic schools.
observations.inference_limit: A broad canon history does not supply a feature-specific Harappan-to-school join.

observations.statement: Skjærvø compares poet-sacrificer roles and the hotar/zaotar, announcement and speech vocabulary across the two traditions.
observations.rival_bearing: R2 supplies an independently motivated verbal/role control.
observations.inference_limit: The comparison uses philological premises; it does not require an excavated teacher for each cognate or identify every technical practice.

observations.statement: The article argues that inherited poet/priest labels acquired negative associations in Old Avestan while related role vocabulary remained.
observations.rival_bearing: A transmitted vocabulary can undergo role evaluation and conceptual change.
observations.inference_limit: Lexical continuity does not imply an unchanged office or unmodified ritual sequence.

observations.statement: The article disputes reading kauui as ruler from later Pahlavi and Perso-Arabic royal sequences back into Avestan.
observations.kind: attributed criticism of a backward interpretation
observations.rival_bearing: Later narrated genealogy can supply R5 framing of older material.
observations.inference_limit: This is the author’s disputed interpretation, not an adjudicated identification of a historical Vištāspa.
